verdicts.summary: Validate is clean (0 errors; the 54 warnings are all conformance/verifies-linkage, one per example) and recipe 7 returns []. Package A is a faithful transcription: all 19 decisions carry a provenance line and the do-nothing option first, the 12 laws are verbatim (Law 4 with its reworded note), F1 to F17 keep the doc's status in measurableBy with the F16 recheck recorded rather than silently applied, and the epic and README state that the owner has ruled on nothing. The E-register is closed both ways (every cited E-number is registered, every registered one is cited), no typed bullet lacks a citation or marker, nothing states ready, nothing is [blocking], and the 9 scoped Specs are exactly the Layer 4 to 6 non-examples, each opening with a deferral line and designing no table or signature. Four major findings stand under the fidelity lens: (1) entityExists is a platform-reserved code in Package C but the kernel reserves only two codes and the adapter has no step that raises it, so three Specs disagree on who rejects a duplicate create; (2) the do-nothing-check decision rules, unmarked, that individual reactions may bypass the obligation module, which the doc frames as a layer-level activation check and which contradicts d13's own alternative bullet; (3) Layer 3 is written at full detail with build-level numbers before the first experiment, against decision-method rule 4, and the deviation lives only in README section 11 rather than on any Spec; (4) a replayed duplicate returns result: null while the declaration's output validator replaces result: v.any(), so a replay fails its own returns validator. Five minor items concern unrecorded costs and small unmarked rulings. None is a blocker; all have concrete fixes.

Convex-correctness review, round 1. Validation is clean (0 errors, 54 conformance/verifies-linkage warnings, all on example Specs). I checked every Convex claim in the Layer 0-3 Specs against the current docs and component READMEs, not memory. Most claims hold: the limits table in F13 matches the limits page exactly (including 30 min Convex / 10 min Node action timeouts and the 5 MiB Node argument cap); scheduling atomicity, exactly-once scheduled mutations, at-most-once actions, no auth propagation, cancel semantics and the 7-day `_scheduled_functions` retention are all as S6 states; OCC retry is automatic and invisible (S1); the React client's retry-until-confirmed with single backend execution and the per-client ordered queue are as S14/S15 state; component sub-transaction isolation, rollback on throw and commit-with-caller are as S2 states; components have no `ctx.auth` and no app env vars, their IDs become strings and their public functions become internal references, as S4 states; `ctx.runMutation` really does take `{ transactionLimits }` (command-pipeline:113 is correct); `ctx.db.system.get("_scheduled_functions", id)` two-argument form exists; `Date.now()` is frozen per function; Workflow (`retryActionsByDefault` false, per-step `retry`, determinism violation on definition change, 8 MiB journal, 1 MB step data) and Workpool (`retryActionsByDefault`, per-enqueue `retry`, `onComplete`, `status().previousAttempts`) match their READMEs; migrations defaults to batches of 100 and iterates only app tables, as E-40 assumes. Three things do not hold. (1) The components authoring page states that the built-in `.paginate()` does not work inside components, yet the context queries contract pins `list` and `history` on `.paginate` and the rebuild and restore batches enumerate through them; the fix is `paginator` from convex-helpers with the same result shape, so it is mechanical, but as written the design contradicts documented Convex behaviour (blocker under this lens). (2) `writeBaseline` is declared as a component `internalMutation`, which the parent cannot reach through `components.x`, while the corpus lists it on the component's API surface and drives it from a parent-side migration; its args also carry no migrated state. (3) Several stated batch and page bounds count documents only and exceed the 16 MiB per-transaction read ceiling at the corpus's own 256 KiB stream budget (200-row list page = 50 MiB, 100-row backfill batch = 25 MiB, 256-stream operation = 64 MiB, 25 folds per restore batch = up to 400 MiB), contradicting the corpus's rule that bounds assume limits add up. Four minor items: the `_scheduled_functions` state is an object `{ kind: "pending" | "inProgress" | ... }` rather than the capitalized strings the operator view types; the 1,000-event fold budget leaves ~390 bytes per envelope and ignores the 1 s query timeout; the receipt row-size claim is 400 KiB in one Spec and 200 KiB in another; the sweeper's 100 nested mutations per run are bounded by documents, not by the 1 s timeout. Nothing found needs an owner ruling; every finding has a local, concrete fix. Not approved until the blocker and the two majors are corrected.

Carrier use is correct and the graph is clean: `sdp validate design` exits 0 with the 54 expected `conformance/verifies-linkage` warnings; recipe 7 (readiness divergence) returns []; every one of the 168 Specs is in exactly one pack with no unresolved members; every `constrainedBy` target is a rule or constraint, every `decidedBy` a decision, every `verifies` comes from an example whose `refines` names the same parent; no Layer 0–2 Spec has an edge into Layer 3–6; every decision Spec lists the do-nothing option first; every E-number cited in a Spec is in the README register and vice versa; every typed bullet carries a citation or marker; `sdp view` renders all 174 pages. Kinds, altitudes and readiness are stated honestly (Layer 4–6 parents `scoped`, no `ready`). The corpus is faithful to the doc and the vocabulary is consistent (no "revision", no receipt-for-evidence, no generation-for-attempt). The problems are cross-package signature and sequence agreement, mostly at the seams Package C, D and E share: who writes read models and with which signature; a replayed duplicate returning `result: null` against a per-command closed `returns` validator; captured facts declared in the kernel and adapter but with no path through the registered operation args or the executor; `entityExists` listed as a closed platform code that no adapter step raises; the write pause being closed "before startGeneration" while the gate must name the generation that is allowed through; the wrapper consuming attempts on `writePaused` so any maintenance window exhausts local reactions, with the two restore switches never sequenced; and `writeBaseline` declared as a component `internalMutation`, which the Convex authoring page says a parent cannot reach. Seven major findings, eleven minor; no blocker. Not approvable under this lens until the majors are reconciled.

Validate: 0 errors, 54 warnings, all conformance/verifies-linkage (accepted). The architecture is sound where it matters: the do-nothing option is first in all 19 decisions and the three design-extension decisions; every Convex fact the corpus leans on (1 s mutation timeout, 30/10 min actions, exactly-once scheduled mutations, at-most-once actions, 7-day _scheduled_functions retention, backups excluding pending scheduled functions, SubtleCrypto and frozen Date.now() in the default runtime, OCC over index-range reads) checks out against the pages, and the online-rebuild race, the receipt read-check-insert race, the write-pause cut and the obligation fences all hold under OCC as written. Every Layer 0 to 2 scenario walks through the design except two that hit contract contradictions: the replayed-duplicate response sets result to null while the public entry's returns validator closes result to the declaration's output schema (Sc L1-3 retry fails return validation at runtime), and the entityExists rejection Sc L1-4 relies on is assigned to an adapter identity check no adapter step performs while the kernel reserves only staleVersion and operationTooLarge. Two cross-package gaps an implementer would trip on: a write pause or restore door turns every pending local reaction's transient writePaused refusals into consumed attempts, exhausting the default budget in about four minutes and parking routine work in needs attention; and the native tier is told to run with production authority while nothing says how a disposable backend mints identities for the public entry. The first experiment is runnable from the corpus once these are fixed; the minors are cost or polish (redundant drain state, a triple-generation write for seven days that the doc does not require, an unbounded fold in restore batches, a sweeper bound that assumes an unmeasured nested-call cost). Not approved under this lens until the four majors are resolved.

Validation is clean (0 errors; the 54 warnings are all conformance/verifies-linkage, one per example), `sdp view` renders 174 pages, and README.md is accurate against the graph: 168 Specs, the per-kind and per-layer census, pack sizes, the 66-Spec/121-question tally, all 323 links, and the plan's section-8 structure all check out. Prose across the corpus is plain: no em dashes outside carrier syntax, no filler, no rejected vocabulary, no `ready` stated. Every PLAN component has its Specs, every one of the 43 scenario rows has its example(s) with bound points, and do-nothing appears first in all 22 decision Specs. Two Convex claims I checked against the pages hold (`ctx.runMutation` takes `transactionLimits`; `crypto.subtle` and frozen `Date.now()` in the default runtime). Layer 0 is implementable as written. Layers 1 and 2 are close, but seven seams between Specs would make an engineer guess or hit a runtime failure: captured facts cannot reach the decider through the pinned `args`; a replayed receipt returns `result: null` against a per-command closed `returns` validator; `entityExists` has three owners; `writeBaseline` has no way to receive the migrated state; the live-update DTO (`R` via `combine`) and the backfill DTO (`toDto`) are never tied together although one `project` must serve both; the pipeline's eleven steps omit the gate read, audit write and diagnostic emit Package D requires and place read-model writes in two incompatible signatures; and several bounds are counted in documents while the same Specs' per-document budgets push them past the 16 MiB read and write ceilings. None is a blocker (each has a small concrete fix and none silently rules on an owner question), but they are major under this lens, so approve=false. Eight minor polish items follow.

Validate: 0 errors, 54 warnings, all conformance/verifies-linkage. All nine round-1 fidelity items are fixed in the text: entityExists has one owner (adapter step 3, E-21, E-39 registered); the do-nothing check is made once per profile; obligation-module and external-effects carry the decision-method-rule-4 question and every Layer 3 child says its numbers are provisional; the replay is a discriminated member of the closed wire type; the two-export cost and its refuted alternative sit on E-7 and d12; journal's by_operation, decider-contract's fact exclusion and write-pause's gate audit are marked [extension] under E-3, E-36 and E-8; the vocabulary names the closed namespace union; the E-44 question states the D4 tension. One note for the orchestrator: the fidelity fixer's note on the migrations batch size says rebuild.sdp.md now cites the @convex-dev/migrations README with a read date, but the file carries the sdp fixer's reading instead (100 is a design number under E-40, not attributed to the component); the concern is resolved either way, only the note is inaccurate. Automated checks are clean: every E-number used in a Spec is in README's register and vice versa, every [extension] bullet carries an E-number, every rule, flow, contract and Design bullet ends in a citation, and every example's outcome is the doc's pass condition verbatim. The new findings all sit on one seam round 1 did not cover, the derived command that a reaction issues through the pipeline: two Specs give it different namespaces (system versus worker), which changes its receipt key; its causation has no path through the pinned internal entry, whose args refuse unknown fields and whose step 7 always mints causedBy of kind command; and its static reactions are said to live on the command declaration, which pins no such field, while the obligation module has the body call createObligation instead. Those three are major. Five minors: two attention reasons beyond D13's four are unmarked; a per-reaction residue in the do-nothing check's consequence; the generations table's Law 11 deviation is not in E-8's question; README's E-25 row still calls writeBaseline an internal mutation; the build tier of Sc L2-4 is not one the acceptance contract names.

Round 2, Convex correctness lens. Validate is clean (0 errors, 54 verifies-linkage warnings). Every round-1 convex fix was re-verified against convex 1.46.0 and convex-helpers 0.1.120 as installed, plus the live docs pages: `paginator(ctx.db, schema)` with `.withIndex` eq/gte ranges and `paginationResultValidator` from `convex/server` exist; `usePaginatedQuery` is exported from `convex-helpers/react`; `writeBaseline` as a public `mutation` is reachable from the parent; `_scheduled_functions.state` is `{ kind: "pending" | "inProgress" | "success" | "failed" (with `error`) | "canceled" }`; `db.system.get(table, id)` exists; `ctx.runMutation` does accept `transactionLimits`; `Date.now()` is fixed and `performance.now()` increments in mutations; `SubtleCrypto` is in the default runtime; the limits page matches section 9 (16 MiB read/write, 32,000 scanned, 4,096 index ranges, 16,000 written, 1 s query/mutation, 30/10 min actions, 1000 schedules per mutation); backups exclude env vars and pending scheduled functions and say nothing about components; the migrations README confirms `batchSize`, `customRange` and the 100 default; the Workflow and Workpool READMEs confirm the S11/S12 facts (determinism violation, 8 MiB journal, 1 MB step data, `retryActionsByDefault` false, per-enqueue `retry`, `status.previousAttempts`, `onComplete`); `withIdentity` exists on `ConvexTestingHelper` for E-13. Three majors remain, all residues of the byte-budget and pagination fixes rather than new mechanisms: `writeBaseline`'s batch bound is stated in documents only and reads 25 MiB and writes up to 50 MiB at the default stream budget; the restore stream-check batch can read about 31 MiB in its worst case although it claims about 8 MiB; and the reactive path the corpus mandates passes `endCursor`, under which `paginator` ignores `numItems`, so the byte-derived `list` and `history` page caps do not bind unless `maximumRowsRead`/`maximumBytesRead` is also passed. Two minors: the rebuild backfill's parent-side read arithmetic is wrong at the 64 KiB row ceiling, and the illustrative parent pass-through query has no `tenantId` in its args.

SDP conformance is clean: `validate design` prints 0 errors and exactly 54 `conformance/verifies-linkage` warnings; recipe 7 returns `[]`; recipe 5 shows five packs with no unresolved members; every example `refines` and `verifies` exactly its parent; every `[extension]` bullet carries an E-number and every typed bullet a citation; every E-number in the corpus is in the README register and every register owner carries its `Extension E-n` open question; the README's census (168/54, 15/6/27/25/22/17/2/54, 159 defined, 9 scoped) and its 67-Spec / 126-question table match the corpus; `sdp view` writes 174 pages; all nine Layer 4-6 Specs open with a deferral line, state `scoped` and lead with a `[deferred]` rule. Every round-1 item under the sdp lens that was marked fixed is fixed in the Specs named (read-model owner, replayed member, facts path, entityExists owner, gate-before-generation, wrapper deferral and restore order, public `writeBaseline`, stale-version mechanism, `DecisionActor`, VersionedResult, executor args, restore door exemption, payload byte check, operator retry, L2-8 assumption), and the journal/F17 rejection is correct (journal cites neither F17 nor Probe 6). What remains are five internal contradictions an implementer would trip on, all introduced or left by the round-1 fixes: the derived mapping's byte budget contradicts its own parts limit; the baseline writer ignores the byte-derived bounds and the 16 KiB payload bound the same corpus made binding; the operator reconcile is dispatched by a path the settle contract fences out and the lifecycle does not allow; the worker authority shape exists in three spellings across actor-and-scope, tenancy-and-authority and the obligation record; and the too-large input bound has two names and two checkpoints. Nine minor items cover leftover signatures, a missing `deferred:` bullet on three rule/workflow Specs, rubric-16 gaps the README claims are closed, and stale README rows.

Validate: 0 errors, 54 conformance/verifies-linkage warnings. Every round-1 "fixed" item under the architecture lens is verified fixed in the current text; every decision Spec leads with the do-nothing option; Layers 0 to 1 and Sc L2-1 to L2-5, L2-7 to L2-9 walk through the design and pass. Seven unrecorded gaps remain that an implementer would trip on, all outside any open question: (1) a live command on a stream the baseline migration has not reached runs the new decider against old-meaning state and re-stamps the schema version so the driver skips it forever; (2) the projection contract has one input shape, one current DTO, so the "cross-stream history" class the write pause exists for, and the cross-context row it names, have no live-path source or backfill form, and the example domain has no such view for L2-6 to exercise; (3) the write pause is keyed by maintained read-model name, so any command that writes a source stream without maintaining the paused view escapes the pause and the consistent cut is not delivered; (4) a tenant-scoped generation switched active blanks every other tenant's rows because the active generation is per read model, not per tenant; (5) operator `reconcile` without evidence schedules the reconcile action directly, and the settle fences on `running`, so the exit from `needsAttention`/`uncertain` never settles; (6) while `OBLIGATIONS_DISPATCH` is off the sweeper, as pinned, rearms every external effect each minute and escalates them all to `recoveryFailing` within about seven minutes of a restore window; (7) restore brings back the gate document's closed entries and in-flight generation rows with no batch, so clearing `MAINTENANCE_MODE` does not reopen a tenant whose rebuild was paused at backup time. Four minors: the baseline driver skips `assertWritable`; the stock stream's `budgetBytes` is never pinned so the 100-line run is `operationTooLarge` at the default budget; the double-submit answer depends on PlaceOrder's unstated context call order; a baseline event bumps the stream version and turns every in-flight reviewed version into `staleVersion`. Not approved until the seven majors are ruled or fixed.

Validate exits 0 with the 54 accepted warnings; `sdp view` renders 174 pages; README links, counts and census all match the corpus. Every round-1 item under this lens is genuinely fixed and the one rejection (journal/F17) is correct. Layers 0 to 2 are implementable end to end for the single-mapping path: signatures, tables, indexes, step sequences, error taxonomy and byte-derived bounds now agree across the kernel, context, command and application families. Three majors remain, all around the baseline migration and the derived mapping, which the round-1 fixes wrote or touched without reconciling against the corpus's own byte rules: E-2 caps a derived stream at 256 KiB in one bullet and 8 MiB in the next; a baseline event's payload holds the whole state while E-12 and `append` bound every payload at 16 KiB and a derived state cannot fit a 1 MiB document; and `limitBaselineBatch` (100 streams, 4,000 events) exceeds the 16 MiB read and write ceilings at the default budget. Seven minors are polish and small cross-Spec disagreements, including three stale README statements the round-1 fixers explicitly left for the README owner.

Round 3, full scope, read in the main thread: all 168 Specs at corpus digest 84253b0d4b3af9e1. Decision method rule 2: every one of the 22 decision Specs lists the do-nothing option first with its standing cost; one mechanism outside a decision Spec, the audit table of E-43, does not weigh Convex's own audit log (minor). Rule 3, the 43 scenarios walked through the design: Layers 0 and 1 pass, and Sc L2-1 to L2-4, L2-7, L2-9, L3-1 to L3-5, L3-8 and ALL-1 pass. Sc L2-5 passes only while the projection does not change, because one projection writes every generation, so a new version rewrites the active generation in place and a rollback is written by the new code. Sc L2-6 does not pass as pinned: the history backfill's cursor names no source, its verify step cannot pass a stream whose last event keys to no row, and the fold is fed in a different order on the live path than on the backfill with no rule that it must not matter. Sc L2-8 passes on the example's dataset and fails for any backup taken after a meaning migration, where the restore's own checks cannot be satisfied. Sc L3-6 fails on its last verification bullet because a lease outlives the running state and blocks the operator. Sc L3-7 reaches the right outcome but not in the order two Specs promise. Layers 4 to 6 carry rules only and design nothing to refute. Rule 5, refutation by a cheaper Convex-native design: the context component, receipts, the two-entry command binding, the gate document, the obligation table and claim, call, settle each survive, with the alternatives they beat recorded; three places lose to a cheaper form and are minors: a derived command nested where a helper call suffices, a history row rewritten once per stream entry, and a paused backfill that takes one stream per batch. One observation for the owner and no finding, since the doc requires it: a derived command's receipt repeats what the wrapper's fence and atomic commit already guarantee on the local path. Item 40 and the first experiment: not runnable from the Specs alone yet. The rebuild needs a tenant list no Spec defines, the native tier has no stated way to interrupt a batch chain or move time, the example domain has no operation that creates stock, and reads of a stream awaiting its baseline are undefined. The eleven round-2 fixes under this lens were checked in the text: ten are confirmed and one is partly applied. Ten majors and eleven minors, all with concrete fixes and none needing an owner ruling. Not approved.

ledger.issue: Three Specs disagree on how a UI double submit of a create is refused (Sc L1-4). outcome-boundary lists entityExists as a PlatformRejectionCode 'thrown by a context's identity check' (E-5), and idempotency-and-receipts says 'the context's identity index makes the second insert a rejection entityExists'. But outcome-model (E-21) reserves exactly two codes, staleVersion and operationTooLarge, and says 'every other code is the context's own'; initial-state says the creation command 'decides against initial() and typically rejects when the state says the subject already exists', i.e. a decider-owned code; and persistence-adapter's step1 to step10 contain no identity check that could raise entityExists. An implementer cannot tell whether the platform or the decider raises it, and the kernel's reserved list and the boundary's closed list conflict. The choice that the second submit is a rejection rather than an idempotent success is also a ruling the doc does not make and is not registered.
ledger.fix: Pick one owner and make the three families agree. Either (a) add a reserved third code to outcome-model E-21, add an adapter step between step2 and step4 that throws entityExists when a command declared as a create loads an existing stream, and cite it from outcome-boundary; or (b) drop entityExists from PlatformRejectionCode, make it a documented context code raised by decide against initial(), and reword idempotency-and-receipts line 92 and the ui-double-submit example accordingly. In both cases register 'second submit answers with a rejection, not an idempotent success' as an E-number with a [non-blocking] Extension question on idempotency-and-receipts.
ledger.note: One owner: entityExists is the kernel's third reserved code (outcome-model E-21), raised by the adapter's step 3 when a create planned at expectedVersion 0 loads an existing row (details.existing, details.current), before decide runs. initial-state's consequence, outcome-boundary's errorCodeEntityExists, idempotency's rule and uiDoubleSubmit bullet, and the L1-4 example now say the same. The 'second submit is a rejection, not an idempotent success' ruling is registered as E-39 with a [non-blocking] Extension question on idempotency-and-receipts and a README register row.

ledger.issue: do-nothing-check rules that 'a local reaction that needs none of the four may stay a plain scheduled mutation with a system-table scan, recorded as a per-reaction choice' and that 'every local reaction declares whether it is an obligation or a plain scheduled mutation'. The doc frames the do-nothing check as a check at activation of Layer 3, confirmed by Probe 7, not as a per-reaction opt-out that a developer decides; a per-reaction plain scheduled mutation escapes Law 8 (every installed durable capability ships recovery, inspection, retention) and Sc L3-7/L3-8 on the developer's judgment. The bullet cites (D13) with no [extension] marker, no E-number and no open question, and it contradicts d13's own alternative bullet, which says the do-nothing option is 'rejected for the durable profile'.
ledger.fix: Either remove the per-reaction opt-out and keep the ruling layer-wide (the obligation module is installed for the durable profile once Probe 7 shows the do-nothing option fails any Layer 3 scenario, which is what d13 already says), or keep it and mark both bullets [extension] with a new E-number (E-59 is free in the E range), add the matching [non-blocking] Extension question, list it in the README register, and state which laws a plain reaction must still satisfy (Law 7 by its own events, Law 8 by inheriting the module's inspect path) so the owner sees the bypass explicitly.
ledger.note: Took option (a): the per-reaction opt-out is removed. do-nothing-check's decision now says the check is made once for the durable profile and every local reaction of an installed durable profile is an obligation (Law 8); the consequence names the platform's own maintenance batches as the only plain scheduled mutations. d13 already said 'rejected for the durable profile' and needed no change.

ledger.issue: The doc's decision method rule 4 says Layers 0 to 2 get full detail, the first experiment runs, and Layer 3 is written from what it showed; the durable-layers preamble says 'the build that triggers a layer writes the rest'. The corpus writes Layer 3 now at 'Detail: full' with build-level numbers (cron every 60 s, grace 120 s, 5 rearms, backoff 1 s x2 capped 1 h, 8 attempts, 64 KiB payload, 16/500/8 fan-out bounds, 30-day horizon, ten indexes) under E-10, E-51, E-52, E-54, E-55, E-57, E-58, and every Layer 3 Spec states defined. The pre-emption is acknowledged only in README section 11 item 10 and PLAN.md section 11 item 10; no Layer 3 Spec carries it as an open question, so the graph does not show it and rubric item 5 ('Layer 3 has what D13 to D15 give') is not met for the numeric extensions. Not blocking, because README records it, but it is the one place where the corpus's detail stance departs from a doc rule without an in-graph record.
ledger.fix: Add to obligation-module and external-effects a '[non-blocking] Decision method rule 4: Layer 3 is written here before the first experiment; the numeric defaults in E-51, E-52, E-54, E-55, E-58 and the index set in E-57 are provisional until the experiment's measurements and Probe 7; the owner confirms that this does not pre-empt the experiment' (mirroring README item 10). Change the eight children's narrative line from 'Detail: full' to 'Detail: full where D13/D14/D15 rule; numbers provisional until the first experiment' and mark each numeric limit bullet as a provisional default. Alternatively downgrade the numeric bullets to [deferred] defaults and keep the structure; either way the deviation then lives in the graph, not only in README.

ledger.issue: A duplicate is answered with duplicateResponse '{ kind: receipt.outcome, result: null, ..., replayed: true }' because receipts are thin (D6), but command-declaration says 'The declaration's output validator replaces result: v.any() in the entry's returns validator, so the wire type is closed per command', and command-pipeline's validatorCommandResponse says the same. A non-nullable output validator refuses null, so every replayed response of a receipted command fails its own returns validator and surfaces as a technical failure, which breaks Sc L1-3's 'one stored outcome' answer and Sc L1-8's disclosure test. The two extensions (E-30 wire shape, E-7/E-38 declaration) were written by the same package and never reconciled.
ledger.fix: Make the response shape honest to D6: declare CommandResponse⟨R⟩ as '{ ... result: R | null; replayed: boolean }' and build the entry's returns validator as v.union(decl.output, v.null()) for result (or make result optional and omit it on replay), state it in E-30's open question and in the command-declaration bullet, and have the retry-after-lost-response example assert result null against that validator.
ledger.note: Verified against docs.convex.dev/functions/validation: a value that does not match `returns` throws. Made the replay a first-class member of the closed wire type. command-pipeline.sdp.md: `CommandResponse⟨R⟩` is now `{ kind; operationId; affected; versions } & ({ replayed: false; result: R } | { replayed: true; result: null })`; `commandResponseValidator⟨R⟩(output)` is a `v.union` of the executed member (`result: output`, `replayed: v.literal(false)`) and the replayed member (`result: v.null()`, `replayed: v.literal(true)`); both entries declare `returns: commandResponseValidator(placeOrderDeclaration.output)`; E-30's open question, step 5 and a new Verification bullet state it. command-declaration.sdp.md Contract now says the `output` validator is the executed member's `result` and `result` is null exactly when `replayed` is true. idempotency-and-receipts.sdp.md `duplicateResponse` names the replayed member and the `v.null()` branch.

ledger.issue: E-7 binds every command to two registered functions (publicCommand and internalCommand). The doc counts registered functions as a standing cost (decision method rule 2) and D7 rejects a per-command body precisely because it 'doubles the functions every command needs'. command-declaration's risk bullet mentions only hand-written export lines; d12's consequence says the standing cost is 'one declaration per command'; the E-7 open question does not record the doubled function count nor the cheaper alternative the doc's own D7 suggests (one public export per command plus one generic internal dispatcher keyed by commandType from the static registry, at the price of losing tsc-typed internal callers for Sc L2-4). Rule 5 asks each mechanism to be refuted against a cheaper design.
ledger.fix: In command-declaration's E-7 open question and risk, state the standing cost (two registered mutations per command) and name the rejected alternative (single public export plus a generic internal dispatcher, as D7's dispatcher already does) with the reason it lost (typed internal callers and the registration check of Sc L2-4). ledger.issue: Two Specs combine into mass escalation during any maintenance window. The wrapper treats every transient `ConvexError` as a retryable attempt: it "increments the attempt count" and reschedules with backoff 1 s × 2 capped at 1 h, 8 attempts by default, so the whole budget is spent in about two minutes. ledger.issue: A local reaction's body issues a derived command through the pipeline, which calls `assertWritable`. While a scope is paused for a cross-stream rebuild (Sc L2-6) or the deployment is under `MAINTENANCE_MODE=restore`, every body throws the transient `writePaused`; the wrapper classifies a transient as retryable, increments `attemptCount`, and with the default backoff (1 s, base 2, 8 attempts) exhausts the budget after 1+2+...+128 s, about 4.3 minutes, moving the obligation to needs attention with reason `exhausted`. A routine pause or a restore whose checks take longer than that parks every pending local reaction in its scope for an operator, which contradicts D13's "a full worker pool delays work and never turns valid intent into a rejection" and defeats Sc L3-3's intent. Restore makes it worse: `rebuildSchedules` reschedules local wrappers immediately while `MAINTENANCE_MODE` is still set, so the restore procedure itself burns the budgets.
ledger.fix: Treat a `writePaused` refusal as a deferral, not an attempt: in the wrapper (and in `claimAttempt`), on `TransientData.code === "writePaused"` leave `attemptCount` unchanged and reschedule at `now + retryAfterMs ?? drainInterval` with the same attempt number, or have the wrapper call `assertWritable(scopesOfUseCase(...))` before step 5 and return without counting. Make `rebuildSchedules` refuse while `MAINTENANCE_MODE=restore`, or order the durable restore so schedules are rebuilt only after the transactional checks pass. Add a rule to lifecycle-transitions that a maintenance refusal is a `pending → pending` reschedule that changes neither attempt number nor attempt count, and cite it from E-51.
ledger.note: Same fix as the sdp write-pause finding: wrapper deferral without counting, lifecycle rule under E-51, rebuildSchedules refusing under MAINTENANCE_MODE=restore, and the restore ordering in both workflows. The write-pause contract also states that a refused local reaction is delayed, not counted.

ledger.issue: E-32 evaluates admission inside the mutation "so that a refusal that throws leaves no consumption behind"; the flip side is that any later throw, including a business rejection or `forbidden`, also rolls back the consumption. A rate or capacity policy therefore counts only successful commands and cannot bound a storm of rejected or unauthorized calls, which is the traffic capacity policies usually exist for. Not a scenario failure (L1-9 passes), but the design should say so or use D7's nested-mutation form for the consumption write.
ledger.fix: Add a rule stating that admission counts committed intent only, and that a policy which must bound refused traffic writes its consumption through a nested `ctx.runMutation` (the D7 form) so it survives the rejection throw; cite E-32.
ledger.note: The observation is right and is now stated; the proposed mechanism was not adopted because it contradicts Convex. S3 (GenericMutationCtx) says a nested mutation 'runs in a sub-transaction, so if it throws, all of its writes will be rolled back', and S10 says nested calls 'run in the same transaction' as the parent: a nested write cannot outlive a parent throw, so a consumption written through nested `ctx.runMutation` would still roll back with the rejection. The correct D7 form is the inverse: the body is the nested mutation and the parent survives, which is the conditional dispatcher. command-pipeline.sdp.md now has an `[extension]` rule (E-32, D7, F3, Law 5): admission counts committed intent only, unauthorized calls never reach step 6, and a policy that must bound refused traffic runs under the dispatcher of `spec:command.outcome-boundary`, never through a nested write in the pipeline; E-32's open question and `admissionHook` carry the flip side, and command-declaration.sdp.md `typeAdmissionPolicy` says a consumption commits only with the command.

ledger.issue: Under real stock contention (more than the two callers the scenarios use) Convex gives up after its bounded OCC retries and fails the mutation with a conflict error. The boundary classifies every non-`ConvexError` throw as a technical failure, so a client receives an opaque error for what is semantically the `capacity` transient the boundary already has. The engine retry is invisible only while it succeeds.

ledger.issue: A backfill batch reads a 100-row page of the context's `by_identity` range inside its mutation, so any live write to any stream in that key range invalidates the batch and it reruns. On a small, hot keyspace the batch can be starved indefinitely; the design's only remedy is the operator's `resumeGeneration` into the same contention. The OCC argument is right; the bound is not adaptive.
ledger.fix: Make the batch size a per-generation field that halves on repeated conflict (Convex reports the conflict error) down to 1, or enumerate stream IDs in a preceding query and point-read each stream in the batch so only writes to those exact streams conflict; record it under E-40.
ledger.note: The bound is now adaptive per generation: batchSize is a field of the generation row (already there), a new [extension] rule under E-40 says only resumeGeneration changes it, lowering it down to 1 on contention; fnResumeGeneration takes batchSize (1..100); the interruption flow and occRace state that the batch's read set is the index range of its page, that a batch that keeps losing fails after Convex's internal retries with the documents-changed error (docs.convex.dev/error, read 2026-09-30), and that this stall is answered by a resume with a smaller bound. Deviation from the suggested fix, on Convex grounds: automatic halving is not possible from inside the batch because a mutation that loses the OCC race never commits and cannot count its own losses, and the exhaustion error goes to the scheduler's Failed state, not to the design's code; the point-read alternative was not taken because a query inside the same mutation shares the read set, a separate transaction would need an action runner, and point reads of the same 100 streams still conflict with writes to them. The E-40 open question records that Probe 6 measures the contention and decides whether an automatic stall check earns its function.

ledger.issue: One sweep isolates each of up to 100 candidates in a nested `ctx.runMutation`, plus 100 lease expiries, inside the 1-second mutation timeout, while F4 says the size of the nested-call overhead is unknown until Probe 3. ledger.issue: Live commands keep writing the retired generation for the whole 7-day rollback period, so every read-model write costs up to three point reads and three writes per command for a week after each cutover. The doc asks only to "keep the old generation for a rollback period"; it does not say live commands keep maintaining it. A cheaper design that passes Sc L2-5 ("cutover and rollback work"): stop writing the retired generation at switch and let rollback re-open it as `building` and run the verify pass, which the version compare makes cheap.
ledger.fix: Record the two options on E-8 as an owner ruling: write-through (instant rollback, triple writes for 7 days) versus stop-and-reverify (rollback takes one verify pass, single write on the steady path); default to the cheaper one unless the product needs instant rollback.

Consequences applied: transition 'retired to verifying by rollback' replaces 'retired to active'; a command writes the active generation and the one in building/verifying/verified only; generationsToWrite makes at most 2 reads and drops retired; limitRegistryReadsPerCommand 2; rollback refused after retireAfter. projection-contract limitGenerationsPerWrite is 2 (1 outside a rebuild). rebuild.sdp.md: the rollback flow is an [extension] that reopens the retired generation as verifying with a fresh verify cursor and finishes with the ordinary switchGeneration; fnRollbackGeneration describes it; limitBuildingGenerations says two generations; new reviewer bullet. ledger.issue: The projection contract's promise is one `project(tenantId, dto, versions)` shared by live update and backfill. But the live path feeds it the decider's result `R` shaped by each operation's `combine` (the decider contract calls `R` 'the DTO the context operation returns'), while backfill feeds it `toDto(state, meta)` from the `list` query (the queries contract calls `toDto` 'the only path from state to a DTO'). ledger.issue: retention-and-restore says `OBLIGATIONS_DISPATCH` is read in `sweep` and that 'the sweeper only inventories while it is off', but the sweeper Spec's steps 1 to 6 never read the switch. As pinned, after a restore (dispatch rows missing, F12) or at any tick while the switch is off, `recoverOne` rearms every pending external obligation by scheduling `claimAttempt`; claimStep2 returns leaving the row pending, its dispatch row goes to `success`, and the next sweep treats 'Success whose obligation is still pending on the same attempt ID' as missing and rearms again, incrementing `rearmCount` every 60 s until the bound of 5 moves the obligation to `needsAttention` with reason `recoveryFailing`. A restore window longer than about seven minutes (grace 120 s plus five ticks) escalates every pending external effect, which is the same failure class as the round-1 write-pause finding, now on the claim path, and contradicts Sc L3-7 ('dispatch waits until the gap is reconciled; identities stay stable').

Alternatively, and cleaner because it needs no sweeper knowledge, make `claimAttempt` while off behave like the wrapper's maintenance deferral: reschedule itself at `limitDeferralDelay` with the same attempt ID and patch `dispatchId`, so its dispatch row stays `pending` and the sweeper leaves it alone by its existing rule; add that as a second cause of the maintenance-deferral transition in lifecycle-transitions under E-51/E-56. The contract says 'a new version is a new generation, never an in-place rewrite' and rebuild repeats it as a rule, yet from the deploy that changes a projection, before `startGeneration` is even called, every live command rewrites the active generation's rows in place with the new version's output and stamps the new `projectionVersion` on them. Queries then read a generation that mixes two row shapes until the switch. Rollback has the same hole from the other side: `rollbackGeneration` reopens the retired generation, 'live commands write it again', and they write it with the new projection, so the generation the operator rolls back to is no longer the old build. Sc L2-5's 'cutover and rollback work' holds only when the projection did not change, which is the one case the generation mechanism is not for. No Spec says which projection code writes which generation. A second gap sits beside it: `startGeneration`, the batches, the restore's inventory and its read-model check take a read model by name, but its projection and sources live only on command declarations, repeated on every command that maintains it, and no Spec says how a name resolves to them.
ledger.fix: Pin one read-model registry in the parent, one constant per read model: its name, its sources and its projections keyed by version. Command declarations list read-model names or reference the constant, so the version and the projection are stated once (D12). `generationsToWrite` returns `{ generation, projectionVersion }` pairs and step 9 writes each generation through the projection whose version the generation row records; the registration check fails when a generation in `active`, `building`, `verifying`, `verified` or `retired` inside its rollback period names a version the registry no longer holds. State the standing cost under E-8 or E-9: the previous projection stays in the code until its generation is purged. Make the L2-5 example rebuild with a changed projection version and assert that the active generation's rows keep the old version until the switch and that the rolled-back generation is written by the old projection.

ledger.issue: A `HistoryProjection` folds events of several streams into one row, and the two paths feed it in different orders. On the live path step 9 calls `applyHistoryProjection` per `streams` entry in the executor's order, command after command, so an order's row sees `OrderPlaced`, its `StockAllocated` events, later `OrderCancelled`, then `AllocationReleased`. On the backfill the rebuild pages one stream's whole history at a time (rebuild flow 'each history batch takes one stream from the enumeration'), so the same row sees every Orders event first and the stock events after, or the reverse. The contract asks only that `project` be 'deterministic in the prior row and the events' with 'version order within each stream'. It never says the fold must give the same row whatever the interleaving across streams, and D2 gives no order across streams to appeal to. A natural projection, where `OrderPlaced` creates the row and a stock event updates an existing one, backfills to a different row than it wrote live, against the contract's own value line that 'a rebuild cannot disagree with a live update'. The doc sends a consumer whose result depends on order to Layer 6's ordered consumer; Layer 2 does not say its history view must not be one. Deletion makes it worse: `null` from `project` deletes the row, and with it the `sourceVersions` that are the fold's only memory. A later event of the same key from another stream, such as `AllocationReleased` after `OrderCancelled` returned `null`, meets no prior row and recreates one, on either path.
ledger.fix: Add to projection-contract under E-9: a history projection's fold is independent of the order in which different streams' events arrive; only the order within one stream is given (D2), and a view whose meaning depends on cross-stream order waits for the ordered consumer of D18. Add to `determinismCheck` a test that folds one key's events in two interleavings and compares the rows, and have the L2-6 example compare a backfilled row with the live-written one. Rule on deletion: either a history row is never deleted once written and carries its own ended state, or the highest folded version per stream moves off the row into a marker, like `projectionMarkers`, that outlives it. State in orders-inventory-example that the order allocation history fold is written to hold under any interleaving, including a stock event arriving before `OrderPlaced`.

ledger.issue: Two parts of the paused rebuild cannot be built as pinned. First, a history view has several sources, the order stream type and the stock item stream type in the example, but `batchCursorValidator` is `{ tenantId, pageCursor, streamId?, eventCursor? }` with no field for the source being enumerated, and `fnHistoryPageCall` names one component query. `historyStep3` says 'it calls `list` with `numItems` 1 from the page cursor to take the next stream' without saying of which context and stream type, so the batch cannot tell where it is among the bindings. Second, `historyVerify` checks one thing per stream: it reads the stream's last event, 'finds that event's row by `keyOf`', and counts a miss when the row is absent or records a lower version. `keyOf` may return `null`, and for many streams the last event's key is `null`: a stock item that was received and never allocated, and every stream whose last event is a `baseline` after a meaning migration. The Spec does not say what verify does then. Read as a miss, the repair refolds the stream, changes nothing, and the next pass counts the same miss, so the generation never reaches `verified` and, since 'writes reopen only after verification', the sources stay closed until an operator aborts. Read as a skip, the stream is unverified. Either way the check proves only that the last event of a stream was folded, not the earlier ones that belong to other keys.
ledger.fix: Add the source to the cursor, an index into the read model's source list, and iterate tenant, then source, then stream, then event page; say so in `tenantIteration` and `historyStep3`. Replace `historyVerify` with a second pass of the same history batches that counts the events `applyHistoryProjection` did not drop: under the pause nothing changes, so a covered generation folds zero events and a miss is repaired by the pass that found it. The state moves to `verified` when a full pass folds none. That needs no row lookup by key and handles a `null` key by construction. State the cost, one more read of every source's history under the pause.

ledger.issue: `rollbackGeneration` takes any read model: it sets the retired generation to `verifying`, 'live commands write it again from that commit', and a verify pass repairs it. For a history view nothing closes the sources: write-pause says no function other than `startGeneration` closes a source scope for a rebuild. So after a rollback the next live command folds its new events onto a retired row that never saw the events between the switch and the rollback, and `applyHistoryProjection` raises that row's `sourceVersions` to the new event's version. The missed events are now 'not above the recorded version' and are dropped by every later fold, and `historyVerify`, which only compares the last event's version, passes. The rolled-back generation becomes active with holes in it and no check says so. projection-contract's claim that 'the live path never meets a non-active generation of a history view because its building generation exists only while its source scopes are closed' is false on this path, and rebuild's own `rebuildClass` bullet says why it matters: 'a live fold onto a row backfill has not reached cannot be told apart from a complete one'.
ledger.fix: Rule one way under E-8. Either `rollbackGeneration` refuses a `pauseRequired` generation with a plain error, and rolling a history view back means a new paused generation at the old projection version; or it closes every source scope of the view in the same mutation, naming the reopened generation, runs its catch-up pass under the pause, and the scopes reopen only after the switch, exactly as a first build does. Correct the projection-contract sentence to match, and add the rollback of the history view, or its refusal, to the L2-6 examples.

ledger.issue: The unfixed half of r2-architecture-history-and-cross-context-projection-has-no-input. The contract still says a cross-context row 'holds one `StreamVersion` per context' and that such a row spreads `rowConventions`, read-models offers 'one cross-context read-model row' as a read, and the declaration says 'a read model fed by several stream types is bound once per source with the same projection'. For a `Projection⟨D, Row⟩` that cannot work: `project(tenantId, dto, versions)` builds a whole row from one DTO, and `applyProjection` writes it with `ctx.db.insert` or `ctx.db.replace`. Bound to two sources, the second entry's row replaces the first, so the row holds one context's fields and one context's version. No form takes two DTOs or merges into a prior row, and the backfill enumerates one source. The only form that can hold two contexts is `HistoryProjection`, which rebuilds only under the write pause, although D9 says a current-state read model rebuilds online. An implementer who wants D8's 'small cross-context view' as a read model has to guess between a history view with a pause it does not need and a form the corpus does not define.
ledger.fix: Take one of the two options the round-2 finding gave. Narrow: state in projection-contract and read-models that Layer 2 pins per-entity, aggregate and history forms, that a small cross-context current-state view is D8's parent query over bounded component reads, and remove 'cross-context row' from the `Projection` bullets, the row conventions and `fnCrossContextView`; record the missing composite form as a [non-blocking] E-9 question. Or add `CompositeProjection`: `project` takes the DTOs of every matching `streams` entry of one command plus the prior row, the write compares `sourceVersions` per stream, and the backfill composes one `list` DTO with bounded `get` reads of the other context in the same mutation, online.

ledger.issue: The round-2 fix made a command migrate a stream on load, so no decision meets state of the wrong meaning, and it made the `rebuild` query answer `awaitingBaseline`. The other reads were left as they were. Between the deploy that raises `stateSchemaVersion` and the end of the sweep, `get` and `list` load a cold stream's row, which holds state under the old meaning, and return `registration.toDto(state, meta)` with the new code's `toDto`. A query cannot write a baseline, and neither `fnGet` nor `fnList` compares the row's `stateSchemaVersion`. So for the length of the sweep every parent query, the read-model backfill and verify batches, which project `list` DTOs, and the restore's read-model check read DTOs computed from state the code no longer understands: wrong values, or a throw where the shape changed. The journal's `migrationWindow` bullet lists what happens in the window for commands and for `rebuild` and says nothing about `get` and `list`.
ledger.fix: Give the journal one read helper, used by `get`, `list` and nothing else, that applies the registered chain in memory when the row is behind the registration: `migrate(saved, [])` is pure, so a migration that does not read history costs no read and no write. For a `readsHistory` migration rule explicitly: `get` reads the tail, bounded by `maxFoldEvents`, and `list` either does the same within its byte bound or the migration's sweep runs under a closed source scope and `list` refuses with a structured answer until it ends. Add the read path to `migrationWindow`, to queries' Contract, and to the L2-7 example: a `get` on an unmigrated stream returns the DTO of the migrated state and writes nothing.

ledger.issue: Two restore checks fail for a deployment that has ever run a meaning migration, and one of them cannot be passed at all. First, queries says a stream still awaiting its baseline is refused by `rebuild` and 'the caller counts either refusal as a journal finding', and `typeRebuildResult` names `awaitingBaseline` among 'what the restore's journal check records as findings'. Restore says 'nobody reopens a deployment that failed a check', and also that a baseline chain in flight at the backup 'is restarted by the operator after the accepted branch'. A backup taken inside a migration window therefore holds cold streams that are findings, the run can never be accepted, and nothing can clear them: commands are refused by the restore door and the baseline driver reads `gateAllows`, which answers not allowed while `MAINTENANCE_MODE` is `restore`. restore's `fnStreamCheckBatch` itself names only `tailTooLong` and `equal` false, so the two Specs also disagree on what the batch records. Second, the read-model check asserts 'a row whose source versions equal the current versions'. The journal's own risk bullet says that after a sweep 'every read-model row whose source the sweep touched has `sourceVersions` one behind its stream until the next command or verify pass rewrites it', and no verify pass runs outside a rebuild. So after any sweep every cold stream's row is a read-model finding and the restore stays closed.
ledger.fix: Make `awaitingBaseline` pending work, not a finding: `streamCheckBatch` counts such streams per stream type on the run record as a `pendingWork` item of a new kind `baselineMigration`, checks their event contiguity without a fold, and the accepted branch tells the operator to restart the sweep, as restore's rule already says. Correct queries' Contract bullet and `typeRebuildResult` to match. For the read-model check, compare fields with the projection of the current DTO and require the row's versions to be at most the current ones; a row that is behind only by baseline events and equal in fields is not a finding. Alternatively have the baseline driver re-project the streams it migrated, which needs `writeBaseline` to return their DTOs, and say which is taken.

ledger.issue: The round-2 ruling that a generation spans every tenant made the rebuild depend on 'the application's tenant list, read in tenant-ID order': `startGeneration` puts the cursor 'at the first tenant' of it, `tenantIteration` moves to 'the next tenant' of it, the restore's checks under `all` iterate it 'the way the rebuild's `tenantIteration` does', the baseline driver runs 'one chain per tenant' because 'the parent, not the component, knows the tenants', and the receipt sweep runs per tenant. No Spec defines that list. The parent's pinned tables are `grants`, `receipts`, `generations`, `projectionMarkers`, `maintenanceGates`, `imports`, `restoreRuns`, `auditRecords` and `personalData`; none enumerates tenants, and `grants` has no index that yields distinct tenant IDs. The L2-5 and L2-8 examples seed two tenants and assert the cursor crosses them, so the first experiment cannot build its rebuild without inventing the table, its index, and what happens to a tenant created while a pass is under way.
ledger.fix: Pin a `tenants` table in the parent on `spec:command.actor-and-scope` or `spec:command.tenancy-and-authority`: `tenantId`, `createdAt`, an index on `tenantId`, written by the command or operator function that creates a tenant, as an [extension] with its register row. State in `tenantIteration` that a pass reads it by index after the cursor's tenant ID, one tenant per step, and rule on a tenant created behind the cursor: on the online path its streams are all created after `startGeneration` and so written live, and the verify pass enumerates again; under a write pause no stream can be created in a closed source. Point the restore's scope, the baseline driver's `driverTenancy` and the receipt sweep at the same table.

ledger.issue: The round-2 fix that makes every reconcile a claimed attempt is right in structure, but the operator's way in is blocked by a lease nobody clears. `claimStep6` sets `leaseExpiresAt: now + leaseMs`, 35 or 15 minutes. Only the transitions into a terminal state clear it (lifecycle's last bullet, `settleStep3`). `settleStep5`, running to pending, and `settleStep6`, running to needs attention, leave it set, and the operator's `step4` patch does not clear it either. `errorCodeLeaseInFlight` is 'thrown by cancel and by reconcile while `leaseExpiresAt` is in the future', with no test of the status. So when an action reports ambiguous within seconds and the settle parks the obligation in needs attention with reason `uncertain`, the operator's `reconcile` and `cancel` are refused for up to 35 minutes although no call is in flight. The L3-6 example's last bullet, a reconcile attempt reports ambiguous and the operator then calls `reconcile` without evidence, fails as written, and Sc L3-4's working operator exit is late by the lease.
ledger.fix: Clear `leaseExpiresAt` on every transition out of `running`: add it to `settleStep5`, `settleStep6` and the lease expiry, and widen lifecycle's last bullet from terminal states to every transition that leaves `running`. Define `errorCodeLeaseInFlight` as `status === "running"` with a lease in the future. Add to the L3-6 example that the operator's reconcile is accepted immediately after the ambiguous settle.

ledger.issue: The native tier is 'a disposable local backend per test' and the contract says nothing about how a test controls time or interrupts work, yet the examples depend on both. Interruption: L2-5 'kills the backend's scheduler after the third batch', L2-8 'stops the scheduler after its first batch', L2-6 'interrupts after the second history batch', L1-3 has 'the harness drops the response'. A local backend offers no scheduler switch, and a restart leaves the pending batch to run by itself, which exercises none of `resumeGeneration`. Time: L3-2 'advances past the grace' of 120 seconds on a 60 second cron, L3-5 'advances past the lease' of 35 minutes, L3-8 'advances 31 days', L3-4 needs eight attempts under a backoff that sums to minutes. No Spec makes any of these constants configurable and every one is read from `Date.now()` inside the function. The first experiment needs the interruptions to pass Layer 2, so it cannot be run from the Specs without inventing a harness, and the Layer 3 examples cannot run in bounded time at all.
ledger.fix: Add a harness contract to `spec:platform.acceptance-contract` as an [extension]. Interruption is a fault flag in the fixture app, a row a named batch or wrapper reads and throws on, never a scheduler kill, so the chain ends the way a developer error ends it and the operator path is what resumes it; a lost response is a caller that discards the result. Time: every duration the design pins, grace, cron interval, lease, backoff, deferral, retention horizons, rollback period, receipt window, is read from one module configuration with the pinned defaults, and a native run that shortens them records 'adjusted configuration' with the values, which the evidence rule already requires. Say which examples run with shortened values and that Sc L2-9's production-configuration run excludes them.

ledger.issue: The adapter's step 1 admits a plan whose planned streams' `budgetBytes` sum to at most 8 MiB, and three Specs give the result as '32 streams at the default 256 KiB budget'. `limitDocumentsWrittenPerCall` then checks, before returning, 'the sum of the saved streams' `budgetBytes` plus every appended event's serialized size' against the same 8 MiB and throws a plain error above it. A plan at the admitted bound always writes at least one event per stream, so it always exceeds the write check: 32 default-budget streams pass step 1 and fail as a technical failure on every call, which a caller retries unchanged for ever. The stated admissions are therefore one notch too high wherever the byte bound, not the count, binds.
ledger.fix: Make the two bounds agree. Either step 1 admits `8 MiB` minus an event allowance of `maxStreams` times the payload bound, and the worked numbers become 31, 15 and so on; or the write check counts each saved stream at its serialized size rather than its budget, which is what the write ceiling measures. State the choice once in the adapter and correct the three worked figures.

ledger.issue: Step 9 calls `applyHistoryProjection` 'for each `streams` entry', and that helper reads and replaces the row once per key per call. `PlaceOrder` at 100 lines returns 101 entries that all key to the same order, so the order allocation history row is read and replaced 101 times in one mutation, about 200 operations and up to 3 MiB written for one row. The cost is recorded nowhere: `limitHistoryFold` counts rows per entry, E-45's four read-model rows per command is silent on repeated writes, and `limitExpectedDocuments` omits the view. The row itself, 100 lines plus 101 `sourceVersions` entries, is over the default `rowBudgetBytes` of 16 KiB and the table bullet declares no budget. And the Specs do not say whether the measured `PlaceOrder` binds the view: it 'exists in the experiment for Sc L2-6, not as an essential read', yet a binding on the declaration is written by every command.
ledger.fix: Have step 9 gather the events of every matching entry of one command per history projection and call `applyHistoryProjection` once, so each key costs one read and one write; say so in `limitHistoryFold`. Declare `rowBudgetBytes` for `orderAllocationHistory`, 64 KiB at the provisional maximum. State in first-experiment whether the Sc L2-3 runs measure `PlaceOrder` with the view bound, and add its row to `limitExpectedDocuments` if they do.

ledger.issue: Under the pause 'each history batch takes one stream from the enumeration' and reads one `history` page of it, so a stream with two events costs a whole scheduled mutation, a `list` call of one item and a `history` call. The pause closes the view's sources for every tenant of the deployment, because a generation spans all tenants, so the outage of those writers lasts as long as the number of source streams times one batch. `limitHistoryBatch` bounds events per batch at 128 by default and the batch uses a fraction of it for short streams. The duration is an unrecorded cost of the mechanism, and a cheaper batch passes the same scenario.
ledger.fix: Let a history batch take streams from the enumeration until its event bound is spent, with the stream and event cursor saved as now, and state the pause's expected duration as a risk on rebuild: source streams and events divided by the batch bound, times one mutation. Point at the registry's per-tenant alternative as the way to shorten the outage per tenant.

ledger.issue: restore says the durable steps run after acceptance 'so no wrapper is rearmed while the door is closed', and `rebuildSchedules` refuses while `MAINTENANCE_MODE` is `restore` 'so no wrapper is rearmed before the transactional restore has accepted its run'. The cron sweeper is not gated: it 'never reads the switch' and reads no door. On its first tick after the snapshot lands every pending obligation's dispatch row is missing, so it rearms them all, and its lease loop hands every running obligation to `expireLease`, which under `reconcileFirst` claims a reconcile that proceeds with dispatch off. Wrappers whose bodies run a derived command are deferred by `writePaused`, so little harm follows, but fan-out bodies create obligations and reconcile reports settle rows on a dataset whose checks have not passed, and the ordering both Specs promise is not what runs.
ledger.fix: Have `sweep` return early, counting everything as `deferred`, while `process.env.MAINTENANCE_MODE === "restore"`, the same read `rebuildSchedules` makes, and say so in the sweeper's Contract and `restoreUse`. Or drop the two ordering claims and state that the sweeper does the rearm and the lease expiry from the first tick, with `rebuildSchedules` as the cursor-driven catch-up. Add the chosen behavior to the L3-7 example.

ledger.issue: Step 1 takes the 100 oldest pending obligations past their grace with `.take(limitSweepBatch)` and a left-alone candidate is not patched, so it stays at the head of `by_status_next_attempt`. When a legitimate backlog of more than 100 dispatches sits past the grace, which is Sc L3-3's condition, every tick reads the same 100 rows, leaves them alone, and never reaches a failed or missing dispatch behind them. Sc L3-2's bounded rearm then waits for the backlog to drain. Nothing is lost, but recovery is blocked exactly when the scheduler is under load.
ledger.fix: Page the scan inside one run: after a page of left-alone candidates read the next page from the last `nextAttemptAt`, while the elapsed guard allows, since a left-alone candidate costs one point read and no nested call. Keep the bound on rearms per run at `limitSweepBatch`. State it in step 1 and in `limitSweepBatch`.

ledger.issue: `derivedCommandCall` runs a derived command as `ctx.runMutation(internal.⟨module⟩.⟨name⟩Internal, ...)` from inside a reaction body that is already the wrapper's nested sub-transaction. The body's throw already rolls back everything the derived command wrote, so the second nesting buys no partial rollback and costs one more nested call per reaction (F4), with a component call nested inside it. `runPipeline(ctx, decl, call)` is a plain parent function with the same typed arguments. Rubric item 23 keeps nested calls for a boundary or a deliberate partial rollback, and neither applies. The extra call is recorded as no cost.
ledger.fix: Call `runPipeline` as a helper from the body, with the declaration imported and the same `PipelineCall`, and keep the internal entry for callers outside a mutation. If the nested form is kept for a reason, state the reason and the cost in E-54.

ledger.issue: A local body returns `HandlerResult` with `CompletionEvidence`, and the kind for committed work is `events: { contextId, eventId, streamVersion }[]`. A body that issues a derived command receives a `CommandResponse`: kind, result, operation ID, affected refs and stream versions, no event IDs. To fill the evidence the body must make an extra `byOperation` component query per context, which no Spec states or counts, or invent the IDs. A body that writes a parent table and no event has no evidence kind at all, although D13 allows 'an identified domain record'.
ledger.fix: Change the `events` evidence to what the command returns, `{ kind: "operation"; operationId: string; versions: StreamVersion[] }`, which `attemptDiagnosis` can still follow through `by_operation`, and add a `record` kind naming a table and an application ID for a body that writes no event, or state that every local body ends in a derived command.

ledger.issue: The wrapper's step 4 and `claimStep4` recheck a `recheckDelegator` authority by calling `authorize` 'with the captured actor and scope'. `AuthorizeInput` requires a `permission`, and neither the obligation record, `HandlerEntry` nor `EffectHandler` carries one, so the recheck cannot be written as pinned. For a body that runs a derived command the pipeline authorizes the same actor anyway, and a revoked grant then surfaces as the rejection `forbidden`, which the wrapper settles as `cancelled`, not as needs attention with `authorityRevoked`.
ledger.fix: Add `permission: string` and an optional `subjectFrom(payload)` to `HandlerEntry` and `EffectHandler`, read by step 4 and `claimStep4`. State that the wrapper's recheck is what routes a revoked delegator to `authorityRevoked` before the body runs, so the pipeline's `forbidden` is not reached on that path.

ledger.issue: E-43 pins an `auditRecords` table that fails closed and does not weigh what Convex already gives, which decision method rule 2 asks of every mechanism. Convex has audit logging: 'Use `log.audit(params)` inside your Convex function', 'Function commit will block on log persistence', delivered 'to a S3 bucket in your own AWS account' (docs.convex.dev/production/integrations/audit-logging, read 2026-10-01). The same page gives the reasons it does not replace the table: it 'requires a Convex Enterprise plan and is only available for dedicated (D1024 and D2048) deployments', and it emits 'on mutations, both on success and failure, and possibly on OCC retries', so an entry does not prove a commit and the operator's queries by operation, subject and request key have nothing to read. The option and those reasons are not on the Spec.
ledger.fix: Add the native option to the E-43 open question as the do-nothing option with the two reasons it is not taken, and note that a deployment on a dedicated Enterprise plan may add `log.audit` beside the table as an export, never instead of it.

ledger.issue: The Inventory context is given 'the allocate and release decisions' and the experiment's only public commands are `PlaceOrder` and `CancelOrder`. Every run starts from 'a fresh disposable backend seeded with the stock items the order needs', the L2-1 example re-sends 'after stock is added' and the L1-12 example names 'a restock'. A stock item stream cannot exist without an event, and Law 1 allows no write outside a sanctioned operation, so the experiment needs a stock-receiving operation and event that the example domain does not name. A test-only seeding function would also break the rule that Sc L2-9's deployment registers none.
ledger.fix: Add to orders-inventory-example a `ReceiveStock` command with a `StockReceived` event, or name the operator operation that creates stock items, and say that the experiment seeds through it. Count it among the experiment's commands in the model's Verification bullet.

ledger.issue: A verify batch 'checks that every stream whose DTO projects to a row has one', 'while a stream whose DTO projects to `null` needs no row'. On a first build that is enough, because a live delete removes a row that exists. After `rollbackGeneration` the retired generation still holds the row of a subject deleted between the switch and the rollback, the verify pass does not look at it, and the reopened generation becomes active showing a subject that no longer projects to a row.
ledger.fix: Have verify call `applyProjection` in backfill mode for a DTO that projects to `null` as well, which deletes the row if present and counts it as a repaired miss, and say so in the verify flow and in the L2-5 example's rollback step.

sessions.summary: Closed review round 2 after the usage-limit stop: checked the 29 findings without a 'fixed' report against the Specs, finished the ones the cross-package fixer never reached, synced README. No lens has reviewed these 29 fixes; round 3 does.

Round 3, lens architecture, full scope, in the main thread. 0 blockers, 10 majors, 11 minors, all open. Ten of the eleven unreviewed round-2 architecture fixes confirmed in the text, one set to partially-fixed. Not approved.
